content: 1. Nabumetone is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) approved by the FDA for the treatment of osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. 2. Common adverse reactions to nabumetone include edema, pruritus, rash, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, flatulence, indigestion, nausea, occult blood in stools, increased liver function test results, dizziness, nervousness, headache, insomnia, somnolence, and tinnitus. 3. The recommended starting dose for nabumetone in adults is 1,000 mg taken as a single dose, with or without food. 4. Some patients may achieve better symptomatic relief with doses ranging from 1,500 mg to 2,000 mg per day, administered as a single or twice-daily dose. 5. Doses exceeding 2,000 mg per day have not been studied, and the lowest effective dose should be used for chronic treatment. 6. Patients weighing less than 50 kg may require lower doses, and the dose should be adjusted based on the patient’s response to initial therapy. 7. Nabumetone is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to the drug or its excipients, as well as in those who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic-type reactions after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. 8. Severe, potentially fatal anaphylactic-like reactions to NSAIDs have been reported in such patients. 9. Nabumetone is contraindicated for the treatment of peri-operative pain in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. 10. Clinical trials have shown that NSAIDs, including nabumetone, are associated with an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, which can be fatal. 11. Patients with known cardiovascular disease or risk factors for cardiovascular disease may be at greater risk, and the lowest effective dose should be used for the shortest duration possible to minimize this risk. 12. Nabumetone can cause serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events, including inflammation, bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. 13. These GI events can occur at any time, with or without warning symptoms, and are more likely in patients with a history of peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding. 14. Patients with a history of peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding who use NSAIDs have a greater than 10-fold increased risk of developing a GI bleed compared to those without these risk factors. 15. Nabumetone should be used with caution in patients with fluid retention, heart failure, or renal impairment, as NSAIDs can lead to renal papillary necrosis and other renal injuries. 16. Long-term administration of NSAIDs has been associated with renal toxicity, particularly in patients with impaired renal function, heart failure, liver dysfunction, or those taking diuretics. 17. Nabumetone should not be used in patients with advanced renal disease unless absolutely necessary, and renal function should be closely monitored if therapy is initiated. 18. Nabumetone may cause serious skin adverse events, such as exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), which can be fatal. 19. Patients should discontinue nabumetone at the first appearance of skin rash or any other sign of hypersensitivity. 20. 21. Nabumetone is not a substitute for corticosteroids and cannot treat corticosteroid insufficiency. Abrupt discontinuation of corticosteroids may lead to disease exacerbation. 22. Borderline elevations of liver function tests may occur in up to 15% of patients taking NSAIDs, including nabumetone, and rare cases of severe hepatic reactions, including jaundice and fatal fulminant hepatitis, have been reported. 23. Patients with symptoms or signs of liver dysfunction should be evaluated for evidence of severe hepatic reactions, and nabumetone should be discontinued if such reactions are suspected. 24. Anemia may occur in patients receiving NSAIDs, including nabumetone, due to fluid retention, GI blood loss, or effects on erythropoiesis. 25. Nabumetone inhibits platelet aggregation and may prolong bleeding time, though its effect is less pronounced and reversible compared to aspirin. 26. Patients with aspirin-sensitive asthma should not take nabumetone due to the risk of severe bronchospasm, which can be fatal. 27. 28. In cases of acute overdose, symptoms such as lethargy, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain are common and generally reversible with supportive care. 29. Management of overdose includes symptomatic and supportive care, with consideration of emesis, activated charcoal, or osmotic cathartics if the patient is seen within 4 hours of ingestion. 30. Nabumetone should be used with caution in elderly patients, as they may be more susceptible to adverse effects, particularly GI bleeding and renal toxicity. 31. There is limited information on the safety and effectiveness of nabumetone in pediatric patients, and its use in this population has not been established. 32. Nabumetone may interact with other drugs, such as ACE inhibitors, diuretics, lithium, methotrexate, and warfarin, potentially leading to reduced efficacy or increased toxicity. 33. Nabumetone should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, and it should be avoided in late pregnancy. 34. It is not known whether nabumetone is excreted in human milk, and a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother. 35. Nabumetone is administered orally, and monitoring of renal and hepatic function, as well as signs of GI bleeding, is recommended during long-term therapy.
